title: Cut It Anywhere
description: The key-card principle: why a cut can never part two neighbouring cards
tryIt: Practise the whole of Cut It Anywhere five times alone with a deck, then perform it for one person at dinner.

concepts.title: How it works: a deck is a ring
concepts.contentHtml:
A spectator chooses a card, loses it in the deck, and then cuts the deck as many times as they like. You find it anyway. The secret is not in your hands; it is in what a cut really does. A cut lifts a block of cards off the top and puts it on the bottom. Nothing is turned over, nothing is swapped, and no card jumps the queue. So picture the deck not as a line with two ends but as a ring: every card has a card before it and a card after it, and the last card is followed by the first. A cut leaves that ring exactly as it was. It only decides where you break the ring open to hold it as a stack.

That gives you a locator. Place a card you know, the key card, directly in front of the chosen card. They are now neighbours on the ring, and no cut can part neighbours. If a cut happens to fall exactly between them, the key card finishes at the bottom of the deck and the chosen card on top; they are still neighbours, because on the ring the bottom card is followed by the top card. Whatever the spectator does, the chosen card is the one that comes straight after the key.

The idea is old. In 1584 the English writer Reginald Scot told his readers that the principal point of juggling with cards was always keeping one certain card either in the bottom, or in some known place of the stock.1 Scot was exposing conjurors, not training them, but his "known card" is an ancestor of the key card you are about to use.

concepts.title: The method: Cut It Anywhere
concepts.contentHtml:
Follow this with a real deck. The example cards are the seven of clubs (your key) and the queen of hearts (their choice), but any cards will do.

  1. Glimpse. Square the deck face down in your left hand. As you tap its edges level, tip the inner end up for a second and read the bottom card: the 7♣. They think you are tidying.
  2. Choice. Spread the cards between your hands and let the spectator take any card, look at it and remember it. (If they take the bottom card, you already know it is the 7♣.)
  3. Split. Square the rest, lift the top half off and put it on the table. Call it A. The cards left in your hand are B, with the 7♣ on the bottom.
  4. Place. Ask them to put their card face down on A, then drop B on top. Now the 7♣ lies directly on their Q♥. Say "I will make room".
  5. Mix. Ask them to cut the deck and complete the cut, as many times as they like.
  6. Find. Take the deck and deal the cards face up in a heap, saying you are watching for a sign from them. When the 7♣ lands, deal the next card face down to one side without looking at it.
  7. Reveal. Ask them to name their card, then turn the face-down card over.

Check it with an actual order. After step 4 the deck reads, top to bottom: the cards of B, the 7♣, the Q♥, then A. If they cut off the first ten cards and put them on the bottom, the deck reads: the rest of B, 7♣, Q♥, A, then those ten. The pair has not moved. If the 7♣ happens to be the very last card you deal, the cut fell in the one gap, and their card is the first card you dealt. Common mistakes: shuffling instead of cutting, and dealing so fast that the key slips by.

concepts.title: Myth check: cutting mixes the deck
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Cut a deck enough times and it must be well mixed.
Reality A cut mixes nothing. It moves where the ring is opened, so neighbours stay neighbours however often you cut.

A 52-card deck can be arranged in 52! ways, a number that starts 8 and runs to 68 digits (about 8 × 1067). Cutting can reach only 52 of them: one for each place you can open the ring. A riffle shuffle is a different animal, because it interleaves the two halves and so usually parts neighbouring cards. That is why this trick asks for cuts and nothing else, and why the spectator must never shuffle. Shuffles get their own skill later.

Wait, really? The oldest advice on this is bolder than you might expect. Scot wrote in 1584 that it will be easy for you to see or spy one card.1 He added that even if you are perceived to do so, it will not be suspected as long as you shuffle the cards well afterwards. Your modern version has the spectator's cuts playing the part of his shuffle: a harmless-looking act of mixing that hides the one thing that matters.

title: Where the Key Comes From
description: Glimpses, crimps and the old art of keeping a known card where you want it
tryIt: Crimp the bottom card of a deck, shuffle nothing, and see whether you can spot the bent corner when you deal the cards face down.

concepts.title: How it works: three ways to know a card
concepts.contentHtml:
A key card only works if you know it, or can find it again. There are three classic ways to get one without anyone noticing. The first is the glimpse you used in Cut It Anywhere: you read the bottom card while squaring the deck. The second is the crimp: you bend one corner of a card by a hair, so that later you can spot it by eye even though you never saw its face. The third is control by shuffling: you keep a known card at the bottom through a shuffle.

Scot describes the third in loving detail. While you shuffle, he says, you keep the bottom card a little before or a little behind the cards lying beneath it, so that a finger can reach it. Then a finger creeps up to meet it, and when you feel it you hold it there until you have shuffled over the cards again, still leaving the kept card below.1 Once you are perfect at it, he promises, you may do almost what you list with the cards.2

He goes further. By this means, Scot says, a packet of eight, twelve or twenty cards can be kept together next to the bottom card while you still shuffle them often to satisfy the curious beholders.3 Read that again with the ring in mind: it is the key-card idea in other clothes, a group of cards that travels with a known card whatever the shuffling looks like. Modern shuffle controls are a skill of their own, so we leave them for later in this course. For now, the glimpse and the crimp are all you need.

concepts.title: The method: Feel the Key
concepts.contentHtml:
This is Cut It Anywhere with one change: you never look at a face. The key card is crimped, not seen, so nobody (not even you) can say you peeked.

  1. Crimp. Hold the deck face down in your left hand. As your right hand squares the ends, press a fingertip on the near corner of the bottom card and curl it up by two or three millimetres: a gentle curve, never a fold. From the front it is invisible; from above you can see a small lift.
  2. Choice. Look at the ceiling while the spectator takes a card from a spread and remembers it. You do not know the face of any card.
  3. Split and place. Lift off the top half (A), let them put their card on it, and cover it with the bottom half (B), exactly as before. The crimped card now lies directly on their card.
  4. Mix. They cut and complete as often as they wish.
  5. Find. Deal the cards face down into a pile, watching the near corners. When the curled corner comes off the deck, deal it as normal; the next card dealt is theirs, so put it face down to one side.
  6. Reveal. They name the card, you turn it over, and you flatten the crimp with your thumb before anyone looks at the deck.

What they see is a stranger dealing a pile of face-down cards without once looking at a face. What you do is watch for one bent corner. Suppose the crimped card is the 9♦ and they chose the K♠: whatever the cuts, the 9♦ is still immediately followed by the K♠. If the crimped card is the last card in the deck, their card was the first one you dealt, at the bottom of your pile. Mistakes: a crimp so heavy that it shows (and marks the card for good), crimping the wrong card, and shuffling.

concepts.title: Myth check: you need a trick deck
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Card tricks need a special trick deck.
Reality Both tricks so far use an ordinary pack, and a book from the 1630s already said so.

The anonymous English book Hocus Pocus Junior, in its 1635 edition, says that a multitude of delightful feats may be performed by an orderly placing, facing, shuffling, and cutting of cards usually played withall. That describes this whole skill: no gimmick, just order, and the cuts do the work for you.

Wait, really? The same page admits that trick cards were around too. It says cards "may be made halfe of one print and halfe of another", so that holding them different ways presents different pictures. Gimmicked cards are nearly four hundred years old, and so is the lesson that the cleverest props are the ones you do not need. A key-card trick that works with a borrowed deck is worth more than one that needs yours.

title: Handling the Spectator
description: Seating, patter and timing: why the trick works on memory and attention, not hands
tryIt: Perform Cut It Anywhere for one person, seated opposite, with at least three cuts, and tell the story as you deal.

concepts.title: How it works: attention and memory, not fast fingers
concepts.contentHtml:
Nothing in Cut It Anywhere is fast. The glimpse takes a second, the placing looks like tidying, and the spectator does most of the handling. So why does it fool people? Psychologists who study magic, such as Kuhn and his colleagues, argue that misdirection works on perception, memory and reasoning, not on the speed of your hands. Three of their points are worth building into every performance.

First, time misdirection. People remember more of an event immediately after it has occurred, as compared to some time later,1 which is one reason magicians typically try to separate in time the method from the effect. In your trick the secret work (the glimpse and the placing) is finished long before the finding, and the spectator's cuts fill the gap. The more cuts, the longer the delay.

Second, relaxation. Kuhn and colleagues note that attentional de-emphasis can occur once a magic trick has been concluded,2 so an audience does not look hard at what you do next. That is why you glimpse the key card while tidying the deck, before the trick has visibly begun, and why a casual "let me square these up" costs you nothing.

Third, the spectator is in charge. They choose the card, they place it, they cut. Your story is true: you never touched their card. The method is never in the part of the trick that they are watching.

concepts.title: The method: staging Cut It Anywhere
concepts.contentHtml:
Use the same moves as lesson one, but now direct the scene like a film-maker.

  1. Seat them opposite. Put the spectator directly across the table, at arm's length or more. Anyone at your side can see the end of the deck when you tip it for the glimpse (see the plan).
  2. Glimpse early. Do it while chatting, as you square the deck, before you say that you are about to do a trick.
  3. Give them the job. Say: "I will not touch your card. You choose it, you hide it, you mix it." Let them place the card on A themselves, and let them do all the cutting.
  4. Stretch the cut. Ask for "once more" two or three times. The delay does the work.
  5. Find it with a story. Deal face up, telling them that you are watching their eyes, not the cards. Keep the rhythm even, and do not slow down at the key card.
  6. Ask before you look. Put the next card aside face down: "I think this is yours, but I have not looked. Tell me your card." Make them say the name before you turn it over.

What they see is a person who never touches their card and never looks at a face. What you do is read one card at the start and watch for it at the end. Common mistakes: telling them what is coming, checking that they are watching, hurrying as the key card goes by, and glimpsing with someone sitting at your side. If you cannot avoid a side seat, glimpse before they sit down, or crimp instead (lesson two).

concepts.title: Myth check: fast hands fool the eye
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Magicians fool you with fast hands.
Reality Nothing in this trick is fast. Attention, memory and timing do the work.

The psychologists divide misdirection into three kinds of mechanism: perception, memory and reasoning.1 Speed of hand is not on the list. A card trick can be fooling a spectator when the performer is standing absolutely still, because the spectator has been steered towards the wrong explanation, or has simply forgotten the moment that mattered.

Wait, really? The idea is ancient in the trade. One writer on magic, Hugard, put it as "magic is misdirection and misdirection is magic",2 and Kuhn and colleagues quote him for it. The remarkable part is how much of this was known by performers long before experiments tested it. Today's research mostly puts names and measurements on what good magicians already did at the table.

For your own practice, that changes what you rehearse. Do not drill speed. Drill the talking: what you say while the spectator chooses, what you say while they cut, and the moment you stop talking to deal. Time yourself, and aim to make the secret work (the glimpse and the placing) take up the smallest and quietest slice of the whole performance.

title: Learning the Card
description: Using the key card as information, and presenting it as a mind-reading trick
tryIt: Practise the Name Game until you can run through the deck in about twenty seconds without losing the order, then perform it once for a friend.

concepts.title: How it works: the key card as information
concepts.contentHtml:
So far the key card has found a card for you. It can also tell you its name. The key card is a known card, and the chosen card sits right after it. So the moment you meet the key in a run of cards, you also see, with your own eyes, the card that follows. You know what the spectator is thinking of, and nobody else does. Present that knowledge as a trick, because it is one: a mind-reading presentation of a simple method, never a claim of real powers.

Scot had a trick in the same spirit, with the title "How to tell one what card he seeth in the bottome, when the same card is shuffled into the stocke". In his version, the performer sees a card privately, lays it undermost, and shuffles until it lies at the bottom again.1 Then he shows it to the beholders so that they remember it, lets anyone shuffle the cards, and tells them what card they saw, since he knew it all along.2 The ring idea is the same: one card you know, and a reason why the shuffling cannot hide it.

The weak point of any mind-reading presentation is the reading itself, so the whole job is to read the card where nobody can see you doing it. Hold the deck so the faces point at you and the backs at the spectator. Look at their face, not the cards, whenever you can. And keep the name back until the very end, so that they have time to forget how you got there.

concepts.title: The method: the Name Game
concepts.contentHtml:
1. Set up. Do steps one to five of Cut It Anywhere: glimpse the key (the 7♣), let them choose (the Q♥), split, place, and let them cut as often as they like.
  2. Note the top card. As you take the deck, glance at the top card and remember it. You need it only in the rare case in step five.
  3. Set the scene. Say: "I am going to look for the trace your card has left. Please do not think of its name." Tilt the deck so that the faces point at you and the backs at them.
  4. Run through. With your left thumb, push cards off the top one at a time into your right hand, each new card going to the back of the packet so that it keeps its order. Read the faces from the top card down, with a glance at the spectator now and then.
  5. Spot the key. When the 7♣ passes, the next card is theirs: the Q♥. Read it, stop, and frown as if you have caught something. If you reach the end and the 7♣ was the very last card, their card is the one you noted in step two.
  6. Reveal in stages. Square the deck, and say: "Red. A heart. A picture card. The queen of hearts." Leave a pause between clues.

What they see is a performer who only ever looks at the backs of the cards in front of them (the diagram shows both views). What you do is read one face. Check it with the order from the diagram: you read 3♠, 9♦, 7♣, and the next card, the Q♥, is the one they chose. Mistakes: reading the faces so slowly that the key card seems to matter, naming the whole card at once, and letting the faces tilt towards a side seat.

If anyone asks how it is done, say that it is a trick. That is honest, and it is a better line than any claim of psychic power.

concepts.title: Myth check: reading your face
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth A mind-reading performer got your card by watching your face.
Reality In the Name Game the card came from a known card sitting next to it. Your face only gave the performer something to look at.

The face-reading story is a classic cover. Whatever the performer seems to be looking at, the real information comes from somewhere you are not watching. In the trick you just learned, it comes from the card before yours.

Wait, really? Scot offered a "mind-reading" stunt of this kind in 1584. He told readers to lay three cards on a table and bid someone think of one, and promised that by his eie you shall assuredlie perceive which he both seeth and thinketh.1 Treat that as a showman's boast rather than a result: he cites no test, and no experiment we use in this course supports it. As a presentation, though, it still works for the same reason as ours: the audience supplies the story, and you supply a quiet certainty.

title: Putting on a Show
description: A short history, then a three-minute routine that uses every find as the next key
tryIt: Perform Three Finds, One Key Chain for two friends, with a different reveal for each find.

concepts.title: How it works: a short history of the trick
concepts.contentHtml:
Where did all of this come from? Playing cards themselves are not European in origin. According to Timothy Husband, a curator at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, card games were introduced to Europe about the middle of the fourteenth century, probably from the Near East via Venice or from the Mamluk sultanate in Egypt. Their arrival was greeted with a spate of bans, and the earliest was issued in Bern in 1367. Tricks followed the cards almost at once, but the earliest English books that explain them were written for a different reason.

The long title of Reginald Scot's book of 1584 promises that "the lewde dealing of witches and witchmongers is notablie detected, the knauerie of coniurors"1 along with much else. The book is, as the title says, a Discoverie of Witchcraft, and the juggling tricks inside it are there to show how supposedly magical wonders are done by sleight. Along the way, it records the key-card idea you have been learning: a card held where you know it will be.

Just over fifty years later, an anonymous book called Hocus Pocus Junior: The Anatomie of Legerdemain (the edition printed in 1635) gave the art a definition: "Legerdemaine is an operation, whereby one may seeme to worke wonderfull, impossible, and incredible things by agility, nimblenesse, and slightnesse of hand." It also says that the art is good and lawful when it is used at festivals and merry meetings to procure mirth. Both rules are still the right ones.

concepts.title: The method: Three Finds, One Key Chain
concepts.contentHtml:
Here is a three-minute routine that uses everything in this skill. The trick is that every card you find becomes the key for the next find, so you never need a new glimpse.

  1. Find one. Cut It Anywhere (lesson one), ending with the found card turned over. Call it F1.
  2. Reset. Square the face-up heap you dealt, turn it over as a block (this undoes the reversal that dealing causes) and drop it on the cards still in your hand. Slip F1 under the deck. F1 is now your known bottom card, and so a new key.
  3. Find two. A new spectator. Split, place and cut as before with F1 as the key, then run through the Name Game (lesson four) and stop when you reach their card, F2.
  4. Reset by cutting. Put the cards you have passed under the cards still in your left hand. That is just a cut, and it puts F2 on the bottom: your next key.
  5. Find three. Crimp the bottom card (lesson two), let a third person choose, place, cut, deal face down, and set aside the card after the curl. This time they name the card before you touch it.
  6. Stop. Three is enough. Leave them wanting one more.

Patter ties it together: "Three people, three cards, and I never saw a face I did not already know." Change the reveal each time, because a repeated reveal teaches the audience how it works. Never repeat a find for the same spectator. If the key is the last card you deal in step one, their card is the first card you dealt; take it out of the heap before you reset. Practise out loud, since half the routine is the talking.

concepts.title: Myth check: Scot wrote a conjuring manual
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Scot's Discoverie of Witchcraft was a handbook for would-be conjurors.
Reality It was written against witch-hunting. The tricks were there to show that wonders can be done by sleight, and Scot refused to show how cheats work.

His chapter on cards is headed "Of cards, with good cautions how to avoid cousenage therein1", and it is full of warnings against gamblers. Scot wrote that he dared not (as he could) show the lewd juggling that cheaters practise,2 lest it give offence to the well disposed, to the simple hurt and losses, and to the wicked occasion of evil doing. We follow the same line in this course: everything you learn is for performing, and nothing here is for use at a card table with money on it.

Wait, really? That means the oldest English instructions for card magic are mixed up with a campaign against persecution. A trick shown honestly, as a trick, was one of Scot's arguments that nobody needed to be burned for doing something a clever amateur could do.
